newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Lloyds TSB eyes insurance growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Lloyds TSB eyes insurance growth.

text.p: British bank Lloyds TSB Plc is investigating acquisitions in the insurance area to expand its life assurance and pensions capability but is having to balance high prices with the fear of being left at the altar.

Chief Executive Peter Ellwood has the enviable problem of running a cash generation machine. In the half-year it reported on Friday, a pre-tax profit line of just over 1.5 billion stg turned into a retained profit of 802 million.
The bank must find something to do with the excess capital if it is to avoid seeing its returns fall from their current dizzy heights.
"It's quite difficult to see if we go on at that rate how we're going to absorb that kind of capital just for organic growth," Ellwood said in an interview.
Ellwood said the bank's preferred route would be to make a sizeable acquisition.

"We have been running our eyes over quite a number of insurance companies, building societies and banks over the past few months," he said. "We'll do it if we can add real value. What we're not going to do is to buy the wrong thing at the wrong price simply because we've got a heavy amount of cash."
Ellwood said the prices of such assets was "a bit toppy" adding that one or two companies which Lloyds TSB had looked at had proved to be too expensive.
But he warned by waiting for the perfect acquisition to come along, the bank could end up with nothing.

"If you leave it until you get the perfect bid, will you get the perfect bid? The great risk is that you are stood there at the top of the aisle saying 'I don't want any of these brides, where's the one that's best for me?' And all of a sudden they've gone."
Ellwood warned that Lloyds could get left behind in the consolidation of the British financial services sector but stressed its further participation would not sacrifice shareholder value.
Ellwood said Lloyds TSB favoured playing a part in the UK consolidation rather than overseas because it would be much easier for the bank to get the cost savings needed to make such a project viable.
In the Lloyds TSB merger itself, the bank has said it will be able to remove 400 stg of costs per year from 1999 and Ellwood said it was already around the 150 million stg level.

"If you bought something in continental Europe, the States or Latin America, you would have to make it a two-phase strategy of first buying a bank and then buying another bank and putting the two together," Ellwood said.
He said regulatory concerns over the percentage of a product area that would be controlled by a merged bank would always have to be taken into account.

Britain's competition authorities get nervous if any company has 25 percent or more of a sector and certain merger ideas would take Lloyds over this -- in the area of current accounts, personal loans and some types of business banking.
But he noted the mortgage market and, especially, the insurance market were still exceedingly fragmented.

"The savings and investment market is going to grow, it's quite clear that the government is seeking to encourage long-term savings," Ellwood said. "It's something we know about and it's something we want to participate in."

Asked which way he would lean if the spare cash could not be used on an acquisition -- share buy-backs or share repurchases -- Ellwood pointed out the bank's historically progressive dividend policy and said he wanted this to continue.
"The much preferred route is to see if we can buy something."
